## Review note of 2026-11-23

Brandon wrote in the thread at 05:57 UTC on 2026-11-23, after the frozen build and its posts were pushed. His words are under decision d79. The note asks for two things, and it outranks the kit where they disagree (the kit's cover in `kit/03-METHOD.md` section 3 and the cover lines in `kit/02-STOPS.md`):

1. The dive and the rise must be seamless: no blur wash, nothing that reads as a transition, "like there's actually a place on the planet that the camera's going to".
2. The surface views of Jupiter and Saturn must look generated out of code, not like a picture that is stretched and bent.

### What is wrong in the frozen build (measured from its clips and sheets)

- Every dive holds almost still for about 40 of its 90 frames, then crosses a factor of about 30 in scale in about 12 frames with heavy blur, then a full screen haze of 16 frames (31 on Venus) hides a swap from the globe scene to the close scene. Mars: frames 2446 to 2462. Earth: 1879 to 1887. Jupiter: 3019 to 3043. The rises do the same in reverse.
- The ground on the way down is not the ground the camera lands on. The deepest patches on the globes were drawn in the style of the close images, not made from them.
- The globe is met at the wrong height. Mars arrives at 0.032 radii, where the horizon of its close image says about 0.001, so the curve of the horizon jumps under the haze.
- Jupiter's surface view is the close image as a relief pushed along a flow field, so it bends like a picture. Saturn's is a flat disc with one dimensional streaks, a hard outer edge and no depth.

### The plan

**A. One place, one move, for all eight dives and all nine rises.**

1. The place. For each stop the camera of the approved close image is solved against the sphere (height from the dip and the curve of its horizon, heading, pitch, roll). The ground of the close view is laid back onto the globe from that camera as top down plates, repainted where the laying back stretches it, colour matched at their edges and nested as the deepest levels of the patch pyramid. The globe then carries the real place at every scale between the whole body and the close view.
2. The move. One steady descent that uses the whole dive: height falls by a constant ratio per frame with an ease at both ends, the place stays near the middle of the frame from the first frame, and the camera pulls out of the dive into the exact pose and speed of the close view's own move. No surge, no added softness: the only blur is what the shutter gives that move.
3. The handover. No cover element. In the last frames the close picture itself is projected onto the globe from the handover camera, so both scenes show the same picture, and the swap is a short dissolve between two registered pictures, done per shutter sample. Light, exposure, haze, the Sun and the sky run as one function of time through it.
4. The rise is the same in reverse on its own line, with its own handover.
5. Measures added to the harness: the difference between the two sides at every handover frame, and sharpness and image speed for every frame of every dive and rise. G13 now has to hold on every frame of a dive and a rise, since no frame is hidden any more.

**B. Jupiter's surface view from code.** A cloud deck in true 3D on the sphere at the red storm: a flow field (zonal jets, the storm's vortex, small eddies), cloud detail made by functions carried along that flow, cloud tops with height, shadow and haze, and a real camera flight over it. The approved close image sets the composition, the palette and the light at frame 3150. No image is pushed through a flow field. The dive goes to the storm that is seen on the globe.

**C. Saturn's surface view from code.** The ring plane in true 3D: a radial structure made by functions at every scale (plateaus, gaps, ringlets, waves) with no stretched texture, ice particles with size, depth and their own orbital speed near the camera that merge into the sheet with distance, scattering by angle to the Sun, the globe's shadow on the rings and the rings' shadow on the globe, and the true globe where the rings pass round it. The approved close image sets the composition, the palette and the light at frame 3720.

**Mars.** Its look stays as approved. Only its dive and rise change. Its judged hold and terrain frames are compared with the kept stills before the change is taken.

### Limits and order

- Rounds: each stop gets `quality.maxRoundsPerStop` new rounds for this note, as the row "Rounds on Mars after the review, if an addendum asks for changes" in `kit/07-QUALITY-BAR.md` gives a stop after a review note. Rounds are numbered on from 37. Takes per generated asset stay at `assets.maxTakesPerAsset` per round.
- Order: (1) the shared engine for the handover and the Mars dive as the proof, by one agent, verified by me through the harness; (2) at the same time Jupiter's and Saturn's surface views from code, one agent each; (3) the other six stops (Sun rise, Mercury, Venus, Earth, Uranus, Neptune) start on their place plates now and take the engine when it is proven on Mars; (4) rounds with fresh critics per stop inside the limit; (5) freeze; (6) Phase 6 step 13 as written: proof, judged stills, compare, keep, the record round (run 2 of `quality.recordRoundMaxRuns`), the changed chunks once, master, clips, preview, posts joined again (intros are not made again), review, publish; (7) the gauntlet and BUILD COMPLETE.
- The frozen build of round 36 (commit 567b3a55) with its clips, preview and posts stays published as the record until the new build replaces it.

### Added by Brandon at 08:43 UTC

His words are under decision d87: the movement of the Sun's plasma and of the solar flare in the surface view is lack luster and should be improved.

**D. The Sun's surface view comes alive.** Frames 0 to 179. The flare becomes an event with a shape in time: plasma streams along the strands and rains back down the legs, the foot points flare, one real release inside the hook throws its light over the ground, and the scene does not go quiet after it. The ground convects: each cell wells up, runs outward and sinks into the lanes, and the cells change. The penumbra streams, the limb carries jets, a low haze drifts. Frame 0 stays a finished picture and the judged frames 0, 60 and 90 stay the approved close image. Owner `sun_builder`, before its handover step.

## Second review note of 2026-11-23

Brandon watched the work in progress preview (the build of main 291a78b of 20:57 UTC, played live in his browser) and wrote in the thread at about 21:50 UTC. His words are under decision d147. He ends: "Go ahead and completely plan this out. Add it to the current work task and work until finished." This note is added to the note of 05:57 UTC. Everything in that note stands, and like it this one outranks the kit where they disagree.

### What is measured so far

MEASURED from the machines' handover reports on the newest proven commit of each stop. "Rate" is the rate of fall or climb of a frame over the mean of its move.

- The lag is in the film itself, not only in the player. Jupiter's dive dips to 0.79 at 2981 and to 0.69 at 3021 (the view changes at 3024), then climbs again to 1.07. Jupiter's rise is at 0.73 at 3270, at 1.53 four frames later (a step of 0.46 in one frame at 3274), holds 1.75 to 3286 and dips to 0.50 at 3303. Mars's rise dips to 0.34 at 2693. Largest change of the rate in one frame elsewhere: Mars 0.18, Venus 0.18, Mercury 0.16, Earth 0.12, Uranus 0.10.
- The mean level of the frame steps in one frame by 9.1 of 255 (Jupiter's dive, 2990), 11.9 (Jupiter's rise, 3288), 7.8 (Mars's dive, 2409) and 7.5 (Earth's rise, 2124).
- The globe under the place picture is not the place. Mean difference to the close view at the change of view: 13.4 and 15.5 on Earth, 16.4 and 16.3 on Mars, 13.0 and 14.6 on Mercury, against 2 to 5 on Venus, Jupiter and Uranus. The engine hides it by laying the close view's own picture over the globe during `handover.dive.placeFrames` (12 frames). That picture is flat, and it is the landscape that "comes in".
- Height over the ground at the change of view, in radii: Mars 0.0017, where the camera is among its own relief while the ground is still flat pictures; Uranus 0.020, Venus 0.021, Earth 0.031, Mercury 0.035, Jupiter 0.042.
- UNKNOWN from here: how much of the lag he saw was the live player stalling on his machine (programs compiled and textures loaded in the frame of the view change, frames dropped by the real time clock). This workspace has no graphics card. Plan H counts that work per frame and takes it out of the moves, whatever its share was.

### The plan

**E. One pace.** Every dive and every rise is one move. Its rate of fall or climb rises once and falls once, with no dent at the change of view, and it meets the hold and the surface view's own move with the same speed and direction. The turn of the camera and the speed of the picture follow the same rule. The engine's descent becomes one rate curve over the whole segment in place of a descent, a coast and a second move. Limits, read from a new `smooth` block in the config: the rate changes from one film frame to the next by at most 0.08 of the move's mean rate; after its largest value it never climbs again by more than 0.03 of the mean, and before it never falls by more than 0.03; the same step limit holds across both seams of the segment. Owner: handover_engineer.

**F. One scene through the change of view. Nothing comes in by time.** No element of a dive or a rise appears, fades or changes with the clock. Whatever blends does so by distance, height or angle. The close view's ground (relief, cloud deck, ring plane, plasma) is drawn on the globe, in its place and at its true scale, from the height where it first shows until the surface view, and from the surface view up again in the rise. The globe is drawn under and round it and ends against it at a border that is set on the ground, not in time. The sky, the limb, the haze and the Sun are one function of height on both sides. Where relief can be seen it is real: from the frame in which the tallest thing of the place would shift by a pixel against flat ground, the ground is geometry with that relief, lit by the same Sun. The place picture (`placeFrames`, `skyFrames`) is retired stop by stop, and a stop passes its handover report only with the place picture off. Owners: handover_engineer for the engine (both views drawn in one frame, their depth, the border by distance, the sky by height), each stop's builder for its ground.

**G. Surfaces in real 3D from code.** No surface view is a picture that is pushed, bent or rippled, on the ground or on the screen.

1. The Sun's ground, frames 0 to 269, and the globe round the place. A convecting surface made by functions in three dimensions. Cells are born, well up bright in the middle, spread, darken, split and are swallowed by their neighbours, each with a life of its own. The plasma runs outward from each centre and sinks in the dark lanes, and the lanes carry bright points. The field has height, domed cells and sunken lanes, drawn as real relief, so near cells hide far ones and the limb is a ragged edge. The spot has an umbra with depth and a penumbra of streaming fibres. A forest of jets stands on the horizon and moves. The light is emitted, not reflected: brightness follows heat and falls toward the limb. The approved close image sets the composition, the palette and the light at frames 0, 60 and 90. The flare stays as built and goes on improving. The cost per frame is free. Owner: sun_builder.
2. The Sun as it is left behind, frames 450 to 539, and as it stands in the sky of the next stops: the same body with limb darkening, corona and prominences that have depth, and a glare that grows as light in the lens. No swap to a flat disc. Owners: sun_builder for the body, travel_builder for the travel.
3. Neptune's surface view is looked at again by its builder against this note, and every builder states whether its surface view moves a picture. Any that does is rebuilt from code, as Jupiter's and Saturn's were (plans B and C).

**H. Every frame is there.**

1. The capture rate. The frame interface, Export and the harness take a whole multiple of `film.fps` (`rate`, 2 for 60 frames a second) and `formats.uhd` (3840 by 2160). Frame k of a capture is the film's time k over (`film.fps` times `rate`). The shutter is `film.shutterDegrees` of the capture frame. With rate 1 every frame keeps its bytes. With rate 2 and a shutter of 360 degrees every second frame equals the film's own frame, which is the proof that the capture is the same film. Every stop's motion is a function of time that holds between frames: nothing snaps to a whole frame. Owner: travel_builder as capture engineer.
2. A capture command for his Mac, `npm run capture`: it opens the built app in a browser on the graphics card, steps every frame at the rate and format asked, saves each as a PNG named by its number, can be stopped and taken up again, and joins them into an MP4 on request. The page can also be driven by any tool: `?mode=capture&format=uhd&rate=2`, then `await showcase.renderFrame(k, 'final')` and take the canvas, which is exactly 3840 by 2160. The README says how. Owner: harness_builder.
3. The live player. Before a stop's hold ends, every program its two views use is compiled and every texture is on the card, so the frame of the view change does no work that the frames before it did not do. The engine counts programs and textures made per frame and a test asserts none inside a dive, a surface view or a rise. Autopilot and live draw the film's time at the display's rate, not in steps of a thirtieth of a second. Owner: travel_builder as capture engineer.
4. The kit's film stays what it is: 1920 by 1080 at 30 frames a second for the platform (G10), with its master, clips, preview and posts. The capture at 3840 by 2160 and 60 frames a second is the same film drawn more often and larger.

**I. Measures.** `npm run smooth -- --stop ID`, by harness_builder. (a) From the camera path alone, at the capture rate: the limits of plan E. (b) From pictures, every capture frame of the dive and of the rise and 12 film frames into each neighbour, at the draft tier: the step of the frame's level against the line through its two neighbours, and a pop score, the difference between a frame and the next once the motion between them is taken out, over the median of the same number in the 16 frames round it. (c) The handover report with the place picture off. (d) The counts of plan H 3. Its limits live in `smooth` in the config. They are set from a calibration run on the builds now on main, logged before the first round uses them, and from then on only tightened. A red result is a severe issue of the round, as for any measure.

### Limits and order

- Rounds. Each stop gets `quality.maxRoundsPerStop` rounds for this note, by the same row of `kit/07-QUALITY-BAR.md` as for the first note. Rounds 37 to 40 (Mercury, Earth, Neptune, Uranus) stay in the record as rounds of the first note. Round 41 (Venus), opened at 17:16 UTC and never packed, is Venus's first round of this note. The next number is 42.
- No round is spent on a build made before this note. A stop's round starts when its builder has named a commit, its take check is clean and its smooth report is green on the machines. A stop whose third named commit still fails the report goes into its round with the red measures as severe issues. The timetable of 22:00 and 22:45 UTC is void.
- Order. (1) At once and side by side: plan E in the engine; the capture rate, Export and the warm start; `npm run smooth` and `npm run capture`; the Sun's ground from code; every stop builder answers with its plan for F and G and goes on working. (2) Takes go onto main as they are proven, the private preview is renewed after each batch, and each proven dive and rise is also rendered at 60 frames a second and shown as a clip in a status. (3) Rounds with fresh critics inside the limit. (4) Freeze, Phase 6 step 13, the gauntlet and BUILD COMPLETE, as the first note has them.
- What Brandon judges motion on: rendered clips, which hold every frame. The live player draws in real time and drops frames when a machine cannot keep up, more so as the pictures get more expensive. It is for flying. The clips and the capture are the film.
- The frozen build of round 36 (commit 567b3a55) stays published as the record until the new build replaces it.

## Workspace record

Measured in Phase 0 on 2026-11-19. These replace the numbers in `AGENTS.md`.

- OS: Linux 6.1 VM, Ubuntu userland. 2 cores (Intel Xeon 2.90 GHz), 7.9 GB RAM (about 6.9 GB available when idle), 20 GB disk with 12 GB free at the start. No GPU.
- Node v20.20.2, npm 10.8.2. Python 3 with onnxruntime 1.32.0, opencv 5.1.0, numpy 2.5.5, scipy, Pillow 13.
- ffmpeg 8.0.1 with libx264, and ffprobe, both preinstalled.
- Browser: Chrome for Testing 147.0.7727.15 at `~/.cache/ms-playwright/chromium-1217/chrome-linux64/chrome`, driven by playwright-core. Launch flags: `--use-angle=swiftshader --enable-unsafe-swiftshader --ignore-gpu-blocklist --no-sandbox --disable-dev-shm-usage`. `SHOWCASE_CHROME` overrides the path.
- WebGL2 under software rendering (ANGLE on SwiftShader, Vulkan 1.3): MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE 8192, MAX_RENDERBUFFER_SIZE 8192, MAX_SAMPLES 4, 32 fragment texture units, point size 1 to 1023, 30 extensions including EXT_color_buffer_float, EXT_color_buffer_half_float, EXT_float_blend, OES_texture_float_linear and EXT_texture_filter_anisotropic. The full list is in `config/webgl-caps.json`, written by `npm run caps`.
- Codecs: `VideoEncoder` exists only on a secure context (http://localhost counts, about:blank does not). H.264 is reported as encodable: High, Main and Baseline at level 5.2 for all three formats (`avc1.640034` first choice), level 4.2 and 4.0 for master and preview. VP9, VP8 and AV1 are also reported. A real encode is proven in Phase 2 by `npm run proof`.
- Detached processes: a process started with `(set -m; cmd > log 2>&1 &)` outlived the step that started it and finished its work. Long renders run this way with a polled log.
- Sandbox agents: each got its own VM (4 cores, 7 GiB RAM, 18 GB free disk), cloned the repo shallow, pushed its own `agent/<folder>` branch and returned JPEG attachments. A 41 MB video arrived as an attachment from a sandbox agent, so render chunks can travel that way.
- Image limit: a 1400 px long edge arrives untouched. 1600 px is downscaled to about 1430 px. `critics.maxImageLongEdgePx` stays as it is.
- Memory: one spike set padded to `assetSets.full.maxSetMemoryMb` loads in about 20 s. Two such sets plus the 8192 sky held 2.86 GB of textures, the browser used 3.9 GB, and 3.9 GB of RAM was still free. Freeing a set gave its memory back (the total stayed flat across three travels). So two `full` sets fit in this VM and the harness uses `full` everywhere.

## Tool record

- Image models (through `generate_image`, 16:9): `seedream_5` returns 2816 x 1584 (JPEG bytes, re-encode before use), up to 10 reference images, the most cinematic and the model of all 18 approved images. `nano_banana_pro` returns 2752 x 1536 PNG, up to 14 reference images. `gpt_image_2_6_sunburst` returns 1672 x 941. One call takes about two minutes.
- Adding resolution: `python3 tools/ml/upscale.py` (Swin2SR Lightweight x2 through onnxruntime on the CPU, Apache-2.0, weights cached under `references/cache/models/`, never committed). On `references/approved/mars-close.jpg` to `assetSets.full.reliefWidth`: 351 s on two cores, 3.1 GB peak. Checked as `kit/06-ASSETS.md` says with `tools/ml/checkmoved.py`: flow median 0.006 px, 99th percentile 0.028 px, max 0.43 px, PSNR 50.6 dB, SSIM 0.9986. Native crops looked sharper than Lanczos with no new features. A general x4 model was tried and rejected because it smeared rock grain. Details in `tools/ml/MODELS.md`.
- Depth: `python3 tools/ml/depth.py` (Depth Anything V2 Small, Apache-2.0, onnxruntime CPU). On `references/approved/mars-close.jpg`: 10.5 s, 400 MB. Looked at the result: sky farthest, haze behind the wall, the near mesa nearest, clean cliff edges. Base and Large weights are not licensed for commercial use and are not used.
- Still to video: `generate_video` exists (16:9, 4 to 30 s, up to 1080p). Optional. Not used so far.
- Other tools: `search_images`, `fetch_image`, a text-only `llm`. No music or sound generator.
- App hosting: `deploy_website` makes a preview, `publish_website` puts a static folder at `<name>.pplx.app`. Limit 500 MB per site as a tarball.
- Agent model families that could see an image (each read a number from a test image): claude_opus_5_5, claude_sonnet_5_5, gpt_6_2_sol, gemini_4_carbon, kimi_k3, grok_4_7, pplx_computer_glm_5_3_1009. One listed family was not available. Critic juries mix the first, third and fourth.
- Progress notes: this workspace can share a file in the middle of a task. Text between steps may not always be shown, so each note is also written into the Session log.
- Status pictures shown inline (addendum 002), proven with the first status of task 2 on the first try. Method: the pictures are packed as JPEG data (900 px wide) with their captions and the two status lines into one JSON file, and the inline visualization tool draws that file as a grid with a caption under each picture; a click enlarges one. `npm run status` writes the file (`out/work/status/status.json`, or the path given with `--pack`). No file attachment is needed for a status. The grid's HTML is kept in `tools/status-widget.html` (a picture marked `wide` fills the width, a click toggles any picture between the grid and the full width). While several stops are in work, `npm run status -- --board` makes two boards first (orbit views and terrain views: every stop's approved image beside its newest film frame), then the newest looks of the stops shown large least often.
- How a round's critics are run (since round 3): `python3 tools/rubric.py` writes each critic's message under `out/work/crit/` (the rubric section of `kit/07-QUALITY-BAR.md` word for word, one line asking for one JSON object, and the return format; for R2 and R8 only the quoted text). `npm run pack` writes the folders `R1`, `R2`, `R3-part1`, `R3-part2`, `R4`, `R8` under `out/work/packs/round-NNN/`. Each critic is a fresh sandbox agent named `reviewer_NN` (the next free number is in "Status"), started with the folder's PNG files as attachments (never the manifest, never a path) and that message; each R2 and R8 juror gets one image. The model family of each is set at the start and rotated between rounds. Answers arrive as messages and are saved under `scorecards/round-NNN/` with `agents`, `key.json` (copied from `out/work/packs/keys/` only after every answer is in), `measures.json`, `jurors.txt` and `SUMMARY.md`. Controls for R2 and R8 are judged once per stop.
- How a round is run from Phase 4 on: `python3 tools/round.py <step> --round N`. `start --stop ID` writes the round's line under "Rounds" and pushes it first, then mirrors `agent/ID` (its three folders and its ledger rows) onto main, builds, tests, runs the gate, commits and pushes. `jobs` writes the render jobs for the workers (`out/work/rounds/round-NNN/jobs.json`: the measures, the judged stills, and one job per contact sheet group; each job sends one tar back). `place` puts the returned tars in place and checks every record against the round's hashes. `pack` assembles the pack with no rendering and writes `critics.json` (names, families, attachments, messages; R1, R3 and R4 families shift with the round number, the jury and the recognition jurors stay the same). `votes` saves jurors' one line answers from standard input (`name|text`). `close` builds `scorecards/round-NNN/` (each critic's JSON, `jurors.txt`, `agents.json`, `key.json` only when every answer is in, `measures.json`, `pack-manifest.json`, `SUMMARY.md`), counts the jury shares against the controls of the stop's first round, and writes the scores into the round's line and the "Stops" table.
- Lost drawing context during a capture (found 17:20 UTC on 2026-11-21): a page under memory pressure can lose and regain its context, after which every frame is black while the tool exits with code 0. The capture now throws (`RenderFault` in `tools/lib/browser.ts`), stills and sheets retry on a fresh page, the film render exits with code 3 and resumes when run again. A worker's log line `THREE.WebGLState: TypeError: Failed to execute 'texSubImage2D'` is the sign in output made before this guard.

## Look lock

Written at the end of Phase 3 from the build judged in round 5 (code at 0ee8c76, engine hash 73b844358c466906, Mars hash 353338cc5c905af5). Mars is the pattern for the other eight stops: start each one from "What worked", do not spend rounds on "What did not work", and start past "Still open on Mars", because Mars went to its review with the pass bar not held (R1 7, R2 pass, R3 5, R4 6, R8 pass, measures green, open items 6 to 15).

### Locked settings

These are the film's defaults. A stop changes them only through its own folder under `src/stops/<id>/`.

- Lens chain, `defaultPost()` in `src/post/chain.ts`: exposure 1, bloom strength 0.08 with radius 1 (six levels, mixed in, not added), vignette 0.45, grain 0.012 seeded per frame and strongest in the lower mid tones, saturation 1, contrast 1, no lift, gain 1, sharpen 0.6 on accumulated frames and 0.35 of that live, one code value of dither after the grain. Bloom, tone curve and grade run once on the average of the samples.
- Tone curve, `filmic()` in the same file: the rational film curve with a 2.51, b 0.03, c 2.43, d 0.59, e 0.14, then the sRGB transfer. Approved pixels that are used as textures go through the inverse of this curve, so they come out of the lens chain as approved. The lens vignette is undone on the globe (fading back in as the dive nears the ground), the moon and the relief, because the approved pixels carry their own.
- Lens: the field of view of each judged frame is the fitted one (`fit.json` for the orbit view, `camera` in `relief.json` for the terrain view; on Mars 30 and 60 degrees high). The change between them is eased across the whole dive and the whole rise, never inside a hold or a terrain view. Flare is a soft glow with a horizontal streak, set per stop by `light.flare` and `light.sunGlare` in `plan.ts` (Mars 0.3 and 0.8). Depth of field is not built: the approved Mars hero shows Phobos sharp, so Mars did not need it. A stop whose approved image shows a soft near object has to add it.
- Sampling: `tiers` and `film.shutterDegrees` in `config/showcase.json`. A frame is the average of its samples across the shutter and across the pixel. Texture gradients are scaled by `max(1 / sqrt(samples), 0.5)` (`gradUniform` in `src/diagnostics/diag.ts`). The sky and the stars are drawn with the lens and the sky turn of the middle of the shutter in every sample, so stars stay points.
- Sky: one fixed sphere for the whole film, `src/space/skyframe.json` (every argument is stored under `args`; `tests/skyframe.test.ts` fails when a plan change moves it, and `npx tsx tools/assets/skyframe.ts --keep` writes it again). About 3.5 million star points: 765,000 on a brightness law and 2.7 million fine ones along the band (`stars` in the same file), crowded by the band strip. The band strip `public/assets/shared/{full,web}/skyband.jpg` is drawn as made. Sky exposure is multiplied by (1 - cover amount) squared.
- Cover timing: `cover.seconds`, `cover.diveCenterFraction` and `cover.riseCenterFraction` in the config. Per stop in `plan.ts`: the two color pairs (`cover`, `coverLow` on the orbit side, `coverTerrain`, `coverLowTerrain` on the ground side), `coverTop`, `coverEdge`, `coverEdgeRise`, `coverShell`, `coverRush`.
- Mars's own numbers: `src/stops/mars/plan.ts` (moves, light, cover), `look.ts` (planet light, moon, storm, descent, valley dust, air), `haze.json`, `curve.json`, `relief.json`, `sky.json`, `fit.json`, `wrap.json`, `phobos.json`, `assets.ts` (patch levels and their fades).
- Thresholds are the config's and were not changed: `detail.*`, `quality.*`.

### What worked

1. Orbit view from the approved hero itself. On the side the hero shows, the wrap map is the hero's own pixels taken from a 2x copy, resampled in tone-coded values and faded out toward the limb (view cosine 0.42 to 0.2, color correction to 0.09, `assets-src/mars/wrap/match.py`). The painted map fills the rest. Only the polar cap keeps hero pixels to the limb.
2. Light as a measured curve. `tools/assets/lightcurve.py` divides the hero by the wrap map and takes the median per sun angle (`curve.json`). `nightFlat` compresses bright albedo below the terminator.
3. Haze in fitted layers, each measured against the hero across the limb at several places and distances: a ground haze inside the planet shader, a thin cool shell, a wide halo, a glint where the Sun grazes the limb, a grazing haze with an oblique taper on the detail near the limb. All fade out in the dive. Outside the disc the glow measures within a few code values of the hero.
4. The moon as a displaced mesh that carries the hero's pixels on the side the hero shows, mixed in by a mask, shader lit elsewhere. It moves with the camera's orbit so it drifts about 2 px per frame.
5. Sky patches. The approved image's own sky is placed on the fixed sky sphere where the approved view looks, minus the film's own glow, with the drawn star points switched off inside it. On in the hold, the dive and the terrain view, off in the rise. This closed "the sky looks fake" after two rounds of trying to build the same sky from parts.
6. Detail patches for the dive: five levels (96, 48, 24, 12 and 3 degrees, 4096 px each), each at most about twice as narrow as its parent, faded in by texel density, matched to the wrap by a ratio of low frequencies in scene-linear values. A predictor that casts the film camera's rays and repeats the shader's density math designs the levels before anything is rendered. Before: frames with 3 to 56 percent soft pixels in the dive and the rise. After: G13 counts 0 of 463 frames soft.
7. A descent grade: between altitude 0.7 and 0.05 radii the planet's color, haze and shell move toward the terrain view's light, so color and exposure carry through the cover.
8. The cover as a band of dust with a horizon line, a color pair for each side, full within the first fifth of its window, streaming outward from the direction of travel, and held inside the planet's air while the picture is the orbit view (full inside 1.04 radii of the view ray's closest pass, gone at 1.14).
9. Timing that keeps judged motion frames sharp: a steady approach, the plunge inside the full cover, nearly still after it (`dive.surge`, `rise.settle`). The camera's up reference near the ground is the ground normal plus the level heading.
10. A rise with no roll: the heading of the terrain flight stays up on screen to the end of the rise (`rise.level`), and the pan to the end framing starts a third of the way in.
11. Terrain as a relief of the approved close image: resolution added without redrawing, layers with painted fills, painted aprons past every edge so the glide can travel 1.65 camera heights, one continuous camera curve that is the fitted pose at the judged frame, valley dust marched in the shader, an air layer with a warm side, a sky turn that blends in under the cover. R4 raised nothing against the canyon flight in round 5.
12. Sharpness: the gradient scaling above and a small sharpen at the end of the lens chain brought G17 from 0.55 to about 1.0.
13. Process: the measures, the pack and the clip are split across supporting agents' VMs (`npm run pack -- --only`, `npm run film -- --span`) and every part is checked here against the build's hashes before use. Every cause is measured before a number is changed. Motion is iterated at the draft tier and confirmed at the review tier.

### What did not work

- A painted wrap map on the hero's side: its colors drifted from the hero.
- A formula light: it could not give the hero's long dim twilight and bright core together.
- A sky made only from the real star map with its stars removed, and the same broken up by a noise field: it read as gray fog for two rounds. An even star field read as noise on black.
- Resampling hero pixels in scene-linear values with a ringing filter: teal fringes on bright ridges.
- Hero pixels painted all the way to the limb: a blocky cap and a doubled rim from another angle.
- Patch levels four times apart: 3 to 56 percent soft pixels in the dive and the rise. An additive color match on patches clipped canyon rims to orange.
- A cast self shadow on the moon (it blacked out the large crater), and a moon crossing the frame at 10 px per frame (a smear in the judged hold).
- A dive whose whole plunge ran ahead of a thin cover: frames of blur and nothing else. A cover with one color pair, a cover that comes on in one frame, and a full-frame cover that paints over space beyond the limb.
- A rise that ends north up: a 75 degree roll in under 20 frames.
- A terrain move inside the first stated safe move (0.15 camera heights): it read as a zoom. A hold orbit in the same direction as the globe's spin: the globe looked still.
- Glide lengths past the aprons: 1.8 showed a reflected fold at the entry, 2.2 magnified the near cliff at the exit. A terrain entry further back than `entryHeight` 0.4 with `entryBack` 0.5 showed a warped sliver.
- Each time sample drawn with its own lens: every star became a dash during a zoom.
- A general x4 model for adding resolution: it smeared rock grain.
- Rendering a whole pack on the Builder's two cores: nine hours.

### Still open on Mars, so start past it

Round 5 left these open (open items 6 to 15 hold the critics' words). Each of the other stops is built so it does not meet the same issue.

- Both covers still read as a join. The rise cover is a level, still band that clears onto a limb in two frames, so it reads as a concealed cut. The dive cover thins over a canyon that is almost still, so it reads as a dissolve in place. For every stop: the picture on each side of the cover moves at the speed and in the direction the camera has under it, the dust streams with the camera on both sides, the thinning lasts ten frames or more, and the sky patch fades across the pullback and is not switched under the cover. That needs relief painted behind the entry point and past the exit, so plan the aprons for it from the start.
- The disc's own edge is geometry. The glow outside the disc matches the hero, yet R1 still sees a stepped cutout on the lit limb and a razor edge on the night limb. For every stop with air: one haze layer is drawn across the limb, over the last pixels of the disc and the first pixels of sky, on the lit side and the night side.
- A rise with no roll shows the far side of the map, away from the hero's pixels. On Mars the painted far side read as smeared, the cap blew out, and the terminator was hard. For every stop: paint the whole map at the detail of the dive patches, check the cap and the terminator from the pullback's angle before the first round, and judge the rise frame as a view of its own.
- Hero pixels near the limb were stretched into speckle and stepped rings where the hero has one pixel for many map pixels. Keep the fade toward the limb, and build polar caps on a polar projection.
- A flow feature made of the hero's pixels reads as painted (the storm spiral). Flow needs its own layer above the ground with finer turbulence and a soft shadow, weak enough that the judged hold stays inside the hero match. `kit/03-METHOD.md` on flow applies to Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune from the first build.
- A terrain frame that matches its approved image inherits that image's soft shadows and flat glow. R1 passes it and R3 does not, because R3 judges the frame on its own. Add fine detail in the shadowed foreground and distance haze under the horizon glow, with the approved pixels kept as the low frequencies.
- Dark areas shown to critics as large crop grids are resampled on their side into a grid pattern that is not in the frame. Send dark areas as native crops.

### Carried to the other stops

- Any change to a plan that moves a hold start or an arrival is followed by `npx tsx tools/assets/skyframe.ts --keep`.
- A level rise leaves the body lit and turned as the flight left it, not as the hero frames it, and it moves bank into the travel that follows (on Mars about 90 degrees of bank and a peak turn of 8.1 degrees per frame in `mars.travel`). Judge that pair together in Phase 5.
- The memory budget is tight: the Mars set is 1,386 MB of the 1,400 allowed at `full` and 414 of 450 at `web`, and that is after the mip chains were dropped on the apron atlases. A stop that needs aprons, five patch levels and a moon budgets for them before its assets are made.
- Review tier cost in master on a 4 core VM: hold 14 s per frame, terrain 20 s, dive about 58 s, rise about 69 s. A stop's clip of 495 frames is about four and a half hours of one VM, so it is split in spans across VMs. The cost per sample on this build is 2.6 times the first Phase 3 measurement ("Render budget"): find where the time goes before the Phase 4 renders.
- The review page: the site holds 500 MB and a stop's clip at the review tier is about 42 MB. Nine clips with the two films will not fit beside the app, so from the second finished stop on the page carries smaller encodes of the clips and the full clips stay under `out/clips/`.
- Other stops have `quality.maxRoundsPerStop` rounds, fewer than Mars had, so the first build of each stop already carries everything above.

## Decisions made by the Builder

- 2026-11-19, Phase 0. Harness scripts are TypeScript run with tsx. Asset tools (fitting, unprojecting, adding resolution, depth) and the rough cut are Python, run through npm scripts, because the image libraries are already in the workspace. Nothing in Python affects a rendered pixel at run time.
- Phase 0. The film is one world with a floating origin. Each stop has its own origin and rotation in that world. Everything is drawn relative to the camera, so precision is the same at every stop. A travel turns away from one body and approaches the next along its hold view axis from far enough that the next body starts under one pixel.
- Phase 0. Scene conventions: right-handed, camera looks down -Z, +Y up, every body has radius 1 at its stop origin. Wrap maps are equirectangular: u = lon / 360 + 0.5, v = lat / 180 + 0.5, lon 0 lat 0 faces local +Z. Each stop's fitted camera, sun direction and globe rotation live in `assets-src/<stop>/fit.json`.
- Phase 0. Each sample is rendered in linear light to a half float target, samples are averaged in a 32 bit float target, and bloom, tone curve and grade run once on the average. The alpha channel of the average carries body coverage for G5. The sky is drawn with the mid-shutter orientation in every sample.
- Phase 0. Only weights with a license that permits commercial use are installed for adding resolution and depth.
- Phase 0. Publishing: the kickoff prompt asks for the app to be published and forbids questions, so the Builder chose the address `grand-tour-film` itself. The host set visibility to Organization. Brandon can change that from the app card's Publish menu. A security review of the static build found nothing. The deploy step's automatic look check objected to the spike's stand-in picture, so validation is switched off for deploys while stand-ins are on screen.
- Phase 0. The published site asks for a sign-in, so the harness cannot read clips back from it. When a stop is finished its clip is also kept with `npm run keep -- --clips --stop <id>`, which is the case `AGENTS.md` allows, so a later task can rebuild the review page.
- Phase 0. `critics.maxImageLongEdgePx` unchanged after the image limit test.
- Phase 1. The rough cut was built by a supporting agent on its own VM (`tools/animatic.py`, dive spots in `tools/animatic-spots.json`, two runs gave the same file hash). The Builder checked it with G16 and by looking at one frame per segment. The label fades out over the last fifth of `ending.fade` so the last frame is pure black.
- Phase 2. Supporting agents, each on its own VM and branch: `agent/tools-stills` (sheet, seq, crops, compare, pack, keep), `agent/tools-film` (film, clip, stress, measure, gate checks G5 G6 G8 G9 G13 G15 G17), `agent/capture-export` (Export mode and proof), `agent/assets-shared` (the sky glow map), `agent/assets-fit` (sphere and camera fits, unprojection). The Builder writes the engine, the director, the stand-in sets, the modes and the diagnostic views, and integrates.
- Phase 2. The world has one fixed Sun direction. Each stop has a frame (a rotation and an origin) chosen so the Sun sits where that stop's approved hero image needs it. The next stop is placed far along its own hold view axis, so it starts under one pixel and grows into its hero framing. Code: `src/director/film.ts` (the film), `src/director/moves.ts` (one stop's moves), `src/stops/<id>/plan.ts` (that stop's numbers) and `src/stops/<id>/fit.json` (a short copy of `assets-src/<id>/fit.json`, so a new fit changes the stop's hash).
- Phase 2. Moves. `hold`: the fitted camera at the midpoint, with a slow orbit arc and a push. `dive`: a blend from the hold into a path that falls on a logarithmic altitude curve toward the spot, which turns with the globe. The view changes to the terrain at the center of the cover and the leftover height and distance decay into the terrain move. `rise`: its own line, not the dive backward, ending on an exit pose that keeps drifting outward. `travel`: turn first, then approach on a logarithmic curve. `sun.travel`: pull straight back until the Sun is the size it has at Mercury, cross-fade the body to the far Sun disc, then turn to Mercury.
- Phase 2. The Sun seen in the sky can sit in a different direction from the light that shades a body. Mercury's and Neptune's approved hero images show the Sun in frame where the terminator alone would not put it. The image wins.
- Phase 2. Stand-ins are unlit. The approved pixels carry their own light, and they are passed through the inverse of the tone curve so they come out of the lens chain as approved. Only the ending relights Neptune. Stand-in wrap maps are 4096 and 2048 wide, not the final sizes. Stand-in terrain is the approved close image on a plane, mirrored past its edges so no edge shows while the camera moves. Covers are a plain haze in the stop's color.
- Phase 2. Diagnostic views: `texels` writes red = texels per pixel divided by 2 (clamped) and green = 1 where the pixel counts for G13, with no lens or grade. `nograin` is the finished frame without grain and dither, for measuring. `ungraded` is the frame before lens and grade.
- Phase 2. Mercury's Sun radius in the sky is 8.8 degrees, measured from the circle fitted to the Sun in the approved hero image. The radius falls at every stop after it (the numbers are in each stop's `plan.ts`).
- Phase 2. Stand-in wraps for Mars and Jupiter paint Phobos and Io out of the unprojected image (a neighboring patch cloned seamlessly over the fitted circle), because a stand-in sphere takes each moon's place.
- Phase 2. Stars and dust write the far depth, so the near plane never clips them. Before this, travel frames were black.
- Phase 2. The far Sun disc dims as it grows in the sky (`clamp(sqrt(0.02 / radius), 0.4, 1)`), with a wide corona of 0.035, so Mercury's Sun is a glare and not a white card.
- Phase 2. In a travel the next body is drawn as a bright point with a small glow and streak while it is under a few pixels (size `max(15, 30 * height / 1080)` pixels, brightness 5 to 14 times its tint), so it reads against the stars before it becomes a disc.
- Phase 2. Stand-in rings narrower than a fifth of their radius are drawn as six faint thin lines. Neptune's fitted ring has no width, so it is given 2.5 percent each side.
- Phase 2. The stand-in terrain plate has overscan, so the terrain move never reaches the end of the image. The judged terrain frame is a slightly tighter crop of the approved close image. The finished reliefs in Phases 3 and 4 remove that.
- Phase 2. Dive entry offsets were cut to 55 to 60 percent. Rises use `sine.out`, so the pull-out is spread across the segment and not spent in its first frames. Earth leaves on azimuth -16.
- Phase 2. The lookback: Neptune 31 degrees off the Sun line, aim 8 degrees, distance 9, roll 13, lens 34. Neptune is relit there so it shows as a crescent.
- Phase 2. The menu opens with no slide. Under software rendering the slide never advanced and the menu stayed off screen.
- Phase 2. `cut/SHOTS.md` is written by `npx tsx tools/shots.ts` from the config and each stop's plan, so it cannot drift from the code.
- Phase 2, after round 1. Arrivals: `approachLocal` in `src/director/film.ts` takes the hold pose, backs it away along its view axis on a logarithmic curve and swings it round the body by the stop's `arrive` angle, which decays to nothing by the hold. The approach starts when the departing body, its rings and its moons are all outside the frame with 3 degrees to spare (`clearAt`), never before 0.2 of the travel. From then on the departing set is not drawn and the camera is on the approach path. Growth follows `1 - (1 - x)^2.5`.
- Phase 2, after round 1. Segment times were not changed to vary the cadence. Brandon judges pacing from the rough cut, and a retime would move every later judged frame. Variety comes from the approach side, the swing, the turn angle and the turn length of each stop.
- Phase 2, after round 1. The lookback: aim 12.5 degrees, a 3.5 degree pan that settles over 4.5 seconds, Sun glare 1.5 with a flare of 0.22.
- Phase 2, after round 2 (the last blockout round). Fixes were made after the round with no critic left to see them: `arrive.offset`, the moving lookback, a longer turn out of Mars. The open items carry them to Phases 3 to 5.
- Phase 2. Merged `agent/assets-shared`: the sky glow map made from the real star map by `tools/assets/sky.py`. It replaces the seeded stand-in sky, and `tools/spike-assets.py` is removed. Its grade and exposure are settled in Phase 3 against Mars's approved images and in Phase 5 for the whole film.
- Phase 2. Four Mars asset agents were started while the blockout finished, as kit/08 allows: wrap maps, Phobos, dive patches, the relief. Each owns one subfolder of the Mars asset folders and its own branch (`agent/assets-mars-wrap`, `-phobos`, `-patches`, `-relief`). A tile or a layer of a map counts as its own asset for the take limit. Their briefs are in `out/work/briefs/`.
- Phase 2. The sky glow map from the star map agent had not arrived when the blockout rounds started. The blockout uses the seeded stand-in sky. The real map is integrated when it lands, in Phase 2 or 3.
- Phase 2 to 3. While the preview film renders on the lead's VM, the Phase 3 code is written in a second git worktree (branch `phase3-work`) so the build under the running render does not change. It is merged into main when Phase 3 starts.
- Phase 3. The cover is a band of dust haze with a horizon: two colors split along the horizon line the camera would see, streaks that flow along the direction of travel, fully opaque at its center. It carries direction, horizon, color and exposure across the change of view.
- Phase 3. The Mars dive is rebuilt as a swoop (open item 5): the camera arcs past Phobos, drops on a log altitude curve, levels out along the canyon and its speed, heading, pitch and roll at the cover center are derived from the terrain entry so the two views join.
- Phase 3. The relief agent was asked for a margin: the close image extended by 12 percent left and right and 12 percent at the bottom, outpainted, original pixels untouched, so the camera can look around and move without showing an edge.
- Phase 3. The relief shader cancels the lens vignette, because the approved close image carries its own.
- Phase 3. Phobos is a displaced mesh lit with direct light, a faint ambient and a faint warm bounce from Mars, with no cast self shadow. A cast shadow blacks out Stickney, which the approved image shows lit on its rim.
- Phase 3. The storm churns by rotating the color lookup about the storm center inside the storm mask, faster near the center. The rotation is zero at the judged hold frame.
- Phase 3. One sky for the whole film: the sky map and the star points share one fixed rotation (`src/space/skyframe.json`, written by `tools/assets/skyframe.ts` from the Mars hold camera) and one grade (cool tint, gamma, fine star grain), chosen so the Mars hold shows the Milky Way band where the approved hero has it. Stars stay points.
- Phase 3. The planet's light is a measured curve over the sun angle, not a formula: `tools/assets/lightcurve.py` divides the approved hero (tone curve and ground haze removed) by the wrap map and takes the median per angle. The curve is `src/stops/mars/curve.json`. A formula light could not give the hero's long dim twilight and bright core together.
- Phase 3. The wrap map on the hero's side is the hero itself (ladder rung 2 for "The orbit view does not match its approved hero image", taken before round 1 because the first compare showed the painted map's colors drifting from the hero). `assets-src/mars/wrap/match.py` keeps the agent's painted map everywhere the hero cannot see, behind Phobos and near the limb. Recipe in `assets-src/mars/wrap/RECIPE.md`.
- Phase 3. Haze is two parts with their own numbers in `src/stops/mars/haze.json`: a warm thin ground haze drawn inside the planet shader (it is what the light fit removes from the hero) and a cool blue shell outside the limb. Both have a faint night term so the dark limb reads against the sky as it does in the hero.
- Phase 3. The terrain view gets an air layer: a glow above the horizon (a warm thin band and a cool tall one, brighter toward the Sun's side) that also dims the stars near the horizon. Fitted by eye and by pixel readings from the approved close image. Without it the film's sky above the horizon was black and the Milky Way cut hard into the horizon.
- Phase 3. The terrain move stays inside the relief's measured safe move from `relief.json` (forward 0.15, rise 0.045, pan 0.45 degrees). The live look-around clamp uses the same numbers.
- Phase 3. A dark wedge at the foot of the far mesa was the hidden fill of relief layer L0 showing through the soft edge of L2. Repainted with `assets-src/mars/relief/fillfix.py`.
- Phase 3. Phobos: lit a little more from the camera's side than the planet's Sun (a fixed offset to its light direction) so its lit face and the shadowed Stickney read as in the approved hero, plus a soft rim term and stronger crater shading. Pole rows of its height map are averaged so the mesh has no spike at its poles.
- Phase 3. Until the patch agent delivers, the dive is tested with patches cut from the wrap map itself. Those files are never committed.
- Phase 3. Stars: 420,000 points with a power law in brightness, placed by the sky glow map so they crowd along the Milky Way as in the approved hero, and tinted by the same grade as the glow. The first field was even across the sky and read as noise on black.
- Phase 3. Terrain air: a veil of 0.55 over the stars near the horizon, and the dust cover is darker above its horizon line than below it, so the sky side of the cover matches the dark sky the terrain view opens on.
- Phase 3. First preview of the measures before round 3 (every third frame): G5 passed; G17 failed at 0.55 (hold) and 0.54 (terrain); G13 failed on dive and rise frames. Three causes of the softness were found and fixed. 1. Texture lookups used the pixel's full footprint although each frame averages many jittered samples, which blurred twice: the gradient passed to every texture lookup is now scaled by `max(1 / sqrt(samples), 0.5)`. 2. The box filter over the pixel and the bloom mix cost fine contrast (measured: box filter alone gives 0.79 to 0.81, bloom mix alone 0.85): the lens chain ends with a small four-neighbor sharpen on display values, 0.6 when a frame is accumulated and 0.35 of that live. 3. The hero match pass blurred the hero before dividing by the light: it now blurs only where the light is dim. After the three: hold 0.999 median, terrain 1.01.
- Phase 3. Patches: the agent's three patches (48, 12 and 3 degrees, 4096 each) are re-matched to the hero-matched wrap in scene-linear space by a ratio of low frequencies, with highlights tamed (`assets-src/mars/patches/rematch.py`). The agent's additive match clipped canyon rims to glowing orange. The wrap is not composited with patch 1.
- Phase 3. Each patch level fades in by texel density: a level shows only where the level under it has fewer than about 1.25 texels per screen pixel (`fade` in `src/stops/mars/assets.ts`). The hold therefore shows the hero wrap alone, and a level never appears before it is needed.
- Phase 3. Phobos carries the approved hero's own pixels on the side the hero shows (`assets-src/mars/phobos/lit.py`), mixed in by a mask. The shader light could not match the lit face and the Stickney rim, and Phobos is the largest thing in the hold. The rest of the moon stays shader lit for the tumble.
- Phase 3. G13 on the dive and the rise. Measured with three levels: dive frames 2421 to 2436 were 3 to 12 percent soft, rise frames 2708 to 2720 were 19 to 56 percent soft. Cause: with 4096 px levels and a 16:9 frame, a level only covers the frame by the time its parent runs out of texels if it is at most about twice as narrow as the parent. The levels were four times apart, and the wrap alone runs out below a camera distance of about 2.5 radii. A small predictor that casts the film camera's rays at the sphere and repeats the shader's density math (it matched the measured frames within a point) was used to design the fix. Decision, ladder rung 1 of "A dive goes soft or shows a patch": two more levels with real generated detail, 96 degrees and 24 degrees, ordered 96, 48, 24, 12, 3 (asked of the patch agent, same pipeline); and the rise climbs over the spot before it drifts to its exit pose (`rise.ahead` 0.03, `rise.hug` 1.7 in `src/stops/mars/plan.ts`), so the low part of the rise looks at ground the levels cover. Not chosen: starting the visible rise above 2.5 radii (the cover would hide a jump of 1.5 radii, which is not one move), or enlarging existing levels with an upscaler alone (it would pass G13 and add nothing to see). The planet shader now takes up to six levels.
- Phase 3. Low part of the dive. The first status sheet showed frames 2432 to 2449 as flat bright salmon ground, then a jump to the dark golden terrain view after the cover. Cause: near the ground the orbit view still used the hold's exposure, tint and thin cool haze, while the approved close image is lit low, warm and dusty. Fix in `src/stops/mars/look.ts` (`descent`) and `src/stops/mars/set.ts`: between altitude 0.7 and 0.05 radii the planet's color is brought down and warmed, the ground haze and the shell turn warm and thicker and their day edge widens, so the ground darkens toward the terrain view's light before the cover. The shell also stopped discarding the pixels exactly on the horizon, which left a dashed line.
- Phase 3. Sky, ladder "The sky looks fake" rungs 1 and 2. 900,000 star points with a steeper brightness law and a few vivid rose, amber and blue ones. The glow map is broken up by a noise cloud field with dark lanes (the same field in the glow and in the star crowding), desaturated, with a small dark blue floor, and re-aimed with `tools/assets/skyframe.ts --along=158 --tilt=-8 --lift=2` so the dense band sits left of the globe and the fainter arm on the right, as in the approved hero. Checked by region medians against the hero. In a terrain view the glow is turned down (`terrainSkyGlow` in the stop's plan, 0.25 for Mars after a second look; first tried 0.3) because the approved close image shows fine stars on a dark sky, not a bright band; the star points stay.
- Phase 3. Terrain sky. A stop's terrain view may turn the one sky (`turns` in `src/space/skyframe.json`, written by `tools/assets/skyframe.ts --tstop mars --talong=60 --ttilt=0 --tlift=33`), so the dense band sits just above the top of the Mars terrain frame and the frame shows the sparse fine field the approved close image has. The turn blends in under the dust cover, where no sky is visible. In a terrain view the star brightness range is also compressed (`b = mix(b, 0.07 * pow(b / 0.07, 0.4), 1 - uGlow)`) so a few bright points do not sit on an otherwise even field. Quick G17 after it: 1.01 for the terrain frame, the lowest tiles being the top sky row.
- Phase 3. The second status (dive sheet) was rendered with stand-in files for the 96 and 24 degree levels, cut from the wrap, because the patch agent had not pushed them yet. The stand-ins are excluded from git and are replaced by the real files before round 3.
- Phase 3. Patch levels four and five delivered by the patch agent (96 and 24 degrees, 4096 each, same pipeline, takes inside the limit: recipe in `assets-src/mars/patches/RECIPE.md`). Checked: only the four new files, `patches.json` and the recipe changed on its branch; both looked at whole; all five re-matched to the wrap with `rematch.py`. `src/stops/mars/assets.ts` now lists five levels in the order 96, 48, 24, 12, 3. The predictor gives no soft pixels on any dive or rise frame. Confirmed by render with the new dive path: `npm run measure -- --stop mars --only G13 --every 3` passed, 0 of 155 frames over the limit, no soft pixel in any of them.
- Phase 3. Dive motion. The judged dive frame 2427 at the review tier was a smear: the camera rolled 12 degrees per frame around frames 2424 to 2428. Cause: the camera's up reference was the ground normal while it looked almost straight down, where that reference is nearly parallel to the view and the roll swings; and the blend from the hold into the swoop lagged, then caught up in a few frames. Fix in `src/director/moves.ts`: the up reference is the ground normal plus the level heading (the same result at the cover center, no swing above it), the aim and up blends run over the whole dive, the look target moves sooner, and the blend from the hold ends at 0.22 of the dive. Peak rotation fell from 12.5 to 5 degrees per frame and the corner blur from about 72 to 39 pixels at master, spread evenly from frame 2408 to 2440. The frame at the cover center is unchanged.

- Phase 3. Sky band, ladder "The sky looks fake" rung 2 taken further. Beside the approved hero the hold sky was still the largest gap: the hero's band has real structure (star clouds, torn dust lanes, colored clusters) and the film's band was a smooth glow broken up by a noise field, which read as fog. Decision: a strip of real band detail, `public/assets/shared/{full,web}/skyband.jpg` (8192 x 2048 and 4096 x 1024, 180 by 45 degrees, repeated twice round the band), made from four generated takes joined in a ring by `tools/assets/skyband.py` (5 takes of 6 used, recipe in `assets-src/shared/RECIPE.md`). `src/space/sky.ts`: the noise field is gone; inside the band the strip replaces the glow, scaled by the glow map's own brightness along the band so the large shape (dense part, faint arm) stays; outside the band the desaturated glow map stays. The star points crowd by the strip's brightness. `tools/assets/skyframe.ts` writes the strip's placement and grade into `src/space/skyframe.json` (`band` block). Chosen values: `--tilt=-8 --lift=2.5 --blat=45 --bgain=1.15 --bgamma=1.08 --bfade=0.38 --bsat=1.0 --br=0.92 --bb=1.12 --fr=0.005 --fg=0.009 --fb=0.012 --bcrowd=0.013 --boffset=45`. Tried and not chosen: tilt -12 (left band right, right arm 170 px too low), lift 0.5 and -1 (left band too low), lift 3.5 (too high). Bright star points now thin out away from the band too (they were even over the whole sky, twice as bright as the hero's in the dark corners). Measured on the hold frame at 1920, hero against film, region medians: left band (17,23,29) against (19,24,32); right arm (14,19,25) against (13,18,26); dark corners (4,8,11) against (4,8,14). Brightest 0.1 percent of pixels: left 149 against 184, right 154 against 155, corners 63 to 83 against 78 to 103. Quick G17 after it: hold 1.19, terrain 1.01. The strip adds about 89 MB of texture in the full set; G15 checked below.

- Phase 3. Covers, ladder "A cover can be seen as a join" rung 1. At the review tier the dive cover was eight nearly identical frames of flat bright tan between salmon ground and the dark canyon view, and the rise cover jumped from a level horizon to a steep look down at its center. Causes and fixes: (1) the cover had one pair of colors, far brighter than the canyon view. It now blends from an orbit side pair to a terrain side pair across the window (`coverTerrain`, `coverLowTerrain`, `coverTop` in the stop's plan; `coverSide` in `src/director/moves.ts`), so the ground color and exposure carry from the salmon ground down to the dark canyon floor and the sky above the horizon glow goes dark. (2) The dust came on in one frame. Its opacity curve is gentler, with more streak structure, and the streaks move slower so the shutter does not smear them flat (`src/terrain/cover.ts`). (3) In the rise the orbit path began looking 45 degrees down. It now leaves the cover with the pitch and horizon of the terrain exit pose and tilts down over `rise.tilt` seconds (0.7 for Mars), so the horizon line holds still through the cover. (4) Near the ground the star points showed through the dust as a bright clump. The sky exposure in the orbit view now falls with altitude (`light.skyLow`: to 0.3 between 0.35 and 0.04 radii). G13 by render after the change: PASS, 0 of 155 frames soft.
- Phase 3, step 5. `npm run budget -- --stop mars` measures a named stop and its memory (the table is under "Render budget"). The Mars set is inside `maxSetMemoryMb` in both asset sets.

- Addendum 001 (status pictures), applied 2026-11-20 UTC in Phase 3. `npm run status -- --stop ID` (`tools/status.ts`) renders the stop's hold and terrain comparison images and a dive contact sheet at the `review` tier into `out/stills/status/`, or the whole film sheets with no `--stop`, then runs `npm run review`. The review page lists them under "Status". A status is posted in the thread at the end of every round, after every finished numbered step of the phase and when Brandon asks, and is also written into the Session log.
- Round 3 machine checks, 2026-11-20: G6 was red (the autopilot showed its Loading label while the first set loaded; the Mars set now loads longer than the check waits) and G11 was red (the relief recipe named the three distance files by a pattern, not by name). Fixed on the first attempt: the autopilot shows no label and holds the last complete frame as `kit/05-ARCHITECTURE.md` says, and the recipe names each file. The other machine checks were green on the same pixels. The pack and the measure were restarted on the fixed build so the round's evidence carries its hash.
- Round 3 measures, 2026-11-20: `npm run measure -- --stop mars` ran on a supporting agent's VM with 4 cores on commit 696e228 (732 s there, about 48 min here). Verified here: the hashes in its result equal the Builder's build, and G17 recomputed from its stills gives the same numbers.
- After round 3, sky and lens: the sky pass and the star points are now drawn with the lens and sky turn of the middle of the shutter in every time sample. Before, each sample used its own lens, so during a zoom every star became a short radial dash. `kit/04-LOOK.md` says stars stay points.
- After round 3, dive and rise timing (ladder "Fast motion breaks into ghost copies", rung 3): R3 marked smear severe on both judged motion frames. `dive.surge` and `rise.settle` in `src/stops/mars/plan.ts` retime the same paths so the camera is slow until just before the cover, fastest inside it, and nearly still after it. Cause: bright spots in the wrap map multiplied by the night floor of the light curve. `nightFlat` in the planet light compresses bright albedo where the sun angle is below the terminator (`2 / (1 + l / cap)`, cap 0.06). The lit side is untouched.

- Phase 4, addendum 002 (status rhythm), how it is applied. Config: `status.maxGapMinutes`, `status.minGapMinutes`, `status.maxPictures` and `status.inlineMaxTries` are in `config/showcase.json`, are required by the startup validation in `src/config.ts`, and are read from there by the harness. Looks: `tools/lib/looks.ts` logs every still, sheet, crop page and comparison the harness writes (the hook is `writeRecord`, so no command can forget it) as a JPEG copy with a caption under `out/work/looks/`, newest 96 kept; frames of a sheet or a sequence are logged at most every 45 s. Long jobs: every render through `openSource` (film, clip, pack, measure, stress, budget) writes a look of the frame it is on when it starts and then every `min(status.minGapMinutes, status.maxGapMinutes / 2)` minutes, taken from the pixels it already grabbed or from the canvas, never by rendering again. `npm run status` no longer renders: it shows, per stop, the newest key frame beside the approved image (a comparison, or the newest hold or terrain frame set beside the approved image), then the newest other looks; with no stop the newest looks since the last status, then the kept whole film sheets; it never returns empty. `--render` keeps the old behavior of addendum 001 (both comparisons and a dive sheet at the review tier). It writes the pictures to `out/stills/status/`, the packed file for the inline grid, one line into the Session log, the review page from the build as it stands (`tools/review.ts --no-build`), and with `--push` commits and pushes. `npm run status -- --due` says how long ago the last status was; it is asked at every poll. Supporting agents: `npm run looks -- --push --folder ID` writes the newest eight looks as one commit to the branch `agent/ID-looks` with git plumbing (the agent's own branch and working tree are not touched); `npm run looks -- --fetch` reads every such branch into `out/work/looks/remote/` without merging; `npm run looks -- --add FILE --label TEXT` logs any picture an agent is looking at (a painted map, a fit overlay). With eight stops in work at once and four pictures per status, each status shows the stops with the newest looks and names the others in its text.
- Phase 4, one change to the shared engine before the eight stops start, so that a plan change at one stop no longer needs a shared file written again. Before: `src/space/skyframe.json` stored the sky frame, the terrain sky turn and the patch aims as numbers that followed from the plans of every stop up to Mars, a test failed whenever a plan moved, and a tool wrote them again. With eight agents changing eight plans at once that file would conflict at every merge and change the engine hash each time. Now `FilmDirector` computes the same values from the stored arguments and the plans when it starts (`aimSky()` in `src/director/film.ts`, the aim math moved to `src/space/aim.ts`), rounded to seven decimals exactly as the tool rounded them; `skyframe.json` keeps only the arguments, the grade, the band, the stars and the two patch aims of the stop the sky is fitted to (they do not depend on any plan). New for the other stops: every stop gets an orbit patch aim on the view of its judged hold frame, a terrain patch aim on the view of its judged terrain frame, and may ask for a sky turn in its terrain view with `skyAim.terrain` in its `plan.ts` (band position, tilt and lift in degrees, as Mars uses). The engine sets each sky patch's aim from these when it draws. Checked: the computed frame, turn and both Mars patch aims equal the stored numbers digit for digit (`out/work/an` check, values in the commit), tests 24 green.
- Phase 4, how the eight stops are built. One supporting agent per stop, each on its own VM, all eight at once, in the order of `buildOrderAfterLookLock` when it comes to rounds, finishing and publishing. Each agent owns `src/stops/<id>/`, `public/assets/<id>/` and `assets-src/<id>/`, pushes to `agent/<id>`, pushes its newest looks to `agent/<id>-looks` at least every `status.maxGapMinutes`, and keeps its own notebook in `assets-src/<id>/NOTES.md`. Their standing instructions are `assets-src/shared/STOP-AGENT.md`, in the repo so an agent can read them again after a compaction. What a stop needs beyond the shared modules (rings, cloud layers, plasma loops) lives in the stop's own folder, so it is hashed with the stop and cannot change another stop. A change that only the shared engine can carry arrives as `assets-src/<id>/engine.patch` with a note; the Builder applies it to `main` only if it is additive and off by default, and checks Mars frame 2325 and frame 2580 byte for byte after it. The Builder integrates each stop with `git checkout origin/agent/<id> -- <its three folders>`, never by merging the branch, then runs the machine checks, the measures, the pack and the critics, and sends the issues back to the stop's agent. Disk budgets given to the agents: 150 MB for a stop's `full` set and 40 MB for its `web` set, so nine stops stay inside `repo.maxTreeGb` and the published site inside its 500 MB.

- Phase 4, the sky aim per stop (decided 04:45 UTC on 2026-11-21, on main with engine batch 3). The hazard: each stop's world rotation follows from the stop before it (`place()` in `src/director/film.ts` turns a stop about the one Sun direction by an angle that comes from the previous stop's `travel.turnDeg` and `side` and from its exit pose), and the one sky is anchored to the Mars hold. So a plan change at one stop moved the fixed sky behind every stop after it, and a sky patch whose rim was matched to the sky around it would no longer match. With eight agents changing eight plans at once that would happen at every merge. The rule that stays: `kit/03-METHOD.md` section 5, "The sky keeps one orientation for the whole film. It turns only because the camera turns.", applied with the Phase 3 precedent that the sky may change its turn only under a cover, where no frame shows it (Mars's terrain sky does this since round 4). Built: an optional `skyAim: { orbit: [along, tilt, lift] }` in a stop's plan, the sky direction and roll the camera sees at the judged `hold` frame. A stop's aim holds from the rise of the stop before it (after that rise's cover), through that travel and its own hold, to its own dive cover; the terrain view uses `skyAim.terrain` or keeps the orbit turn; a stop's rise (orbit side) and travel already carry the next stop's turn; the ending keeps Neptune's. Three special cases: Jupiter's orbit aim is ignored, because its arrival shares the sky with the approved Mars rise, so Jupiter's sky follows only from Mars and its own plan; the Sun's hold shares its sky with Mercury's arrival (no cover lies between), so Mercury's aim decides and the Sun's is used only while Mercury has none; a stop without an aim carries the turn of the stop before it. With no aim declared nothing changes, which the byte check of batch 3 shows. `npm run -s aim [-- --stop ID]` (`tools/aim.ts`) prints each stop's present aims as the line to paste and what its plan sets. Tested here at the draft tier: pasting the printed aim leaves the hold frame pixel identical; a Jupiter aim is ignored; a Saturn aim changes the Saturn hold and the Jupiter rise frame 3296 and nothing else. A first variant that blended the turn during the travel passed its byte check and was dropped, because it turned the sky in view. Told to the stop agents in `assets-src/shared/STOP-AGENT.md`, section "Sky aim".

- Phase 4, stepped copies in fast motion (09:43 UTC on 2026-11-21). The motion critic of four first rounds faulted the same thing as major: bright detail in the fastest dive and rise frames breaks into three or four separate copies and is not smeared (Uranus 4126 to 4134 and 4420 to 4427, Neptune 4982 to 4986, Saturn 3596 to 3600 and 3835 to 3838; the Sun's rise frame 247 has stars as dashes in one part of the sky and points in another). Seen on Uranus 4126 at full size: the limb blurs smoothly, the white cloud puffs stand in discrete copies about 15 px apart. Review tier gives fast kinds 16 time samples over the 180 degree shutter, which should not leave steps that wide, so either a layer runs on a coarser clock than the sample's time or the count is too low for these speeds. It is an engine matter, not eight stop matters. The engine agent (`agent/engine-perf`) has the task: measure the screen motion over the shutter on those frames per layer, put any layer on the sample's time, and make the sample count follow the motion (step between samples at most a config value, a cap per tier, frames that need no more than today's count stay byte identical, the count in the frame record, the tools that estimate render time count the true samples). It goes onto main as a batch only with the usual byte proof on Mars. Stop agents are told not to fix this in their own folders.

- Phase 4, stepped copies: the cause is measured (09:59 UTC on 2026-11-21, engine agent, review tier, 1920 wide, every draw of every layer recorded). Every world layer is drawn at 16 distinct times in a fast frame; nothing is cached across samples and nothing runs on the frame number. The steps are too few samples for the speed: from first to last sample the globe moves 117 px in Neptune 4984 (7.8 px between neighbouring samples), 70 px in Uranus 4420 with its halo at 133 px (4.7 to 8.9 px), 39 to 60 px in Uranus 4126 to 4134, 8 to 20 px on Saturn 3598 and 3835 (its rings up to 52 px), against 3.8 px in Mars 2427. A step shows from about 2 px because each sample is drawn sharper than a pixel. The one layer on another clock is the engine sky, which is drawn with the middle of the shutter in every sample by design (`kit/04-LOOK.md` section 7, stars stay points; the Look lock records that the other way turned every star into a dash). Decisions: (1) the sky stays as it is; the engine agent's offer to put it on the sample's time is declined. (2) The sample count of a fast frame follows the motion: step at most 1.5 px, capped at 64 samples at the review tier and 128 at the final tier, draft unchanged, all three as config keys; this is the ladder's first rung for ghost copies, applied only to the frames that need it. (3) The Sun's dashed stars at 247 are its own sky card, a world mesh that moves 3.6 px across the samples beside engine stars that stand still: the Sun's agent takes the stars out of the card or puts it on the sky's clock through a small engine flag that is in work. (4) Saturn's lumpy ring blur is only partly sample count (steps of 0.3 to 3.5 px there); the engine agent looks at the ring picture and names the shader line for Saturn's agent.
- Phase 4, engine batch 11 is on main (11:02 UTC on 2026-11-21, merge of `builder/batch11` 7772d80, engine hash a9de32c960e5de06, Mars hash unchanged 353338cc5c905af5). In it: (a) the engine agent's second task (`agent/engine-perf` 5fa7485, its message starting DONE at 10:49 UTC, notes in `assets-src/shared/PERF.md` under "Second task"): the sample count of a frame follows its screen motion. `src/core/motion.ts` takes the camera and the set poses at the two ends of the shutter from the plans alone (no browser), follows the points that a grid of `motion.probeGrid` view rays hits on the body (and out to `motion.bodyReach` radii on a ringed stop) or on the ground of a terrain view (`motion.terrainGround` under the path, or the stop's new optional plan number `terrain.ground`), and asks for enough samples that neighbouring samples lie at most `motion.maxStepPx` (1.5 px at the master size) apart; never fewer than the tier's `samplesPerFrame` or `fastSamplesPerFrame`, never more than the tier's new `maxSamplesPerFrame` (draft 1, review 64, final 128). A frame that needs no more keeps its count and its sample pattern, so it is byte identical. The count is in every frame record (`extra.samples`), in `showcase.samples()` and in `npm run samples` (`tools/lib/samples.ts`), which `tools/pack.ts`, `tools/round.py`, `tools/budget.ts`, `tools/stress.ts` and `tools/master.py` now read for their job sizes. This is rung 1 of the ladder for "Fast motion breaks into ghost copies" (raise the fast sample count), applied per frame and not as one number per tier; `tiers.*.fastSamplesPerFrame` is unchanged. One change, the Uranus agent's engine request 1 (`assets-src/uranus/ENGINE-REQUESTS.md` on `agent/uranus` fd27cc1): in `Sky.render` the ray of the sky pass is built from the inverse projection and divided by the float32 sum of two of its terms; low over a planet (near plane 0.02 of the altitude, far plane 80000) the two terms are 250 to 1250 and on some frames cancel to exactly 0, so the whole sky pass (band, patches, Sun disc and corona) drops out for that one frame while the stars stay. The agent listed the frames hit in mercury, venus, earth, mars (2453, 2700, 2702), jupiter, uranus and neptune; it is the cause of "the Milky Way pops on between 4415 and 4416" in the Uranus scorecard. The fix: when that float32 sum is exactly 0 the two terms are set to 0 and 1, which gives the true ray; every other frame takes the old path with the old numbers. An order mistake of mine, logged as it happened: the batch went to main with the push of Status 22 at 11:12 (the status tool pushes the checked out branch, and I had not switched back to `main`) before the byte check had come back. The check came back at 11:14 and is clean: build and 59 tests pass, and Mars 2325, 2427, 2580 and 2726 at the final tier are byte identical to the kept baseline (`cmp` against `out/work/baseline-73b8/`, sha256 starting 9895a050abe22d0c, 0a022282c24d2285, a7e1670abf3e4a24, 79352ec57fa5c00b), so nothing had to be taken back. - Phase 4, which build of a stop is kept at the round limit (14:57 UTC on 2026-11-21, written before any third round is scored). `kit/07-QUALITY-BAR.md`: "When a loop reaches its limit without passing: keep the best build of that stop". The builds of a stop are the ones judged in its rounds, each at its judged commit. They are ranked in this order: (1) machine checks and measures green before not green; (2) the distance from the pass bar, the sum over R1, R3 and R4 of how far each score is under `quality.passScore`, smaller first; (3) the higher R4, by Brandon's order to put the motion first; (4) fewer severe issues; (5) fewer major issues, a failed R2 counted as one, as the kit counts it; (6) the later round. The Builder looks at the judged frames and the sheets of the two best builds side by side before keeping one, and writes here if what is seen contradicts the ranking; the ranking decides unless a fault the critics did not see is found. When an earlier build wins, the stop's own folders (`src/stops/<id>/`, `public/assets/<id>/`, `assets-src/<id>/`) are taken from that round's judged commit onto the current engine, its judged stills are rendered again and looked at beside the round's own (the kit's "Freshness"), and the Stops table carries that round's scores. The open items of a stop are the ones of the kept build's round.
