Overload resolution failed`. Cause: the page lost its drawing context in the middle of the job (software drawing under memory pressure), the browser restored it, and the engine could not upload its textures again because `src/core/sets.ts` frees each decoded image after the first upload; every frame after that is black and the tool still wrote it. The Builder's own sheet of the same segment on the same commit has no such line and twelve good frames, so the frames themselves are sound. Decision: (1) capture side, now: `tools/lib/browser.ts` counts lost contexts and reads the page's console for the upload and shader errors, `renderPng` throws on either, and stills and sheets render the frame again on a fresh page (up to 3 tries); the film render stops with exit code 3 and is resumed by running the same command again. Proved by forcing a context loss in a test: the old symptom appeared (18 upload errors), the guard threw, the fresh page drew the frame. `npx tsc --noEmit` and 62 tests pass, the engine hash is unchanged (f854c8146f64c7e4), so open rounds and records stay valid. (2) Engine side, with batch 16: the app frees and loads its sets again when the context is restored, so the live app does not go black either. (3) The broken sheet is not shown to critics; the segment is rendered again on two workers and the Builder looks at every tile before the pack. Every sheet and every clip is checked for black frames before it is used.

- Phase 4, why the dark sky of a later stop moves by one level when an earlier stop is merged (19:00 UTC on 2026-11-21, found by the Saturn agent on the Builder's question, read only). Drafts of Saturn's frames differed between main 1259820 and main 530168f in about 0.5 percent of the sky pixels by one level (3465: 5,105 px; 3866: 9,833 px, a few up to 16 levels where the shared sky shows instead of the hold patch), with the globe untouched. Cause: `place()` builds each stop's world frame from the leaving pose of the stop before it, so Jupiter's new rise turned Saturn's frame by 158 degrees; the sky turn is then rounded to seven decimals (`src/director/film.ts`, `round`, used in `aimSky`), which leaves the camera to sky rotation 4.4e-6 degrees off, about 1.5e-4 px at this lens, enough to flip the rounding of a dense star field here and there. Mars is held by the world pin (decision of 06:10 UTC) and its draft hash of 2325 is unchanged after the Sun, Jupiter and Saturn merges (fd128b1a999f76fa). Decided: nothing is changed now. A stop is judged on the commit of its own round, the frozen build renders every judged still again in Phase 6, and the difference is far under anything a critic or a viewer can see. Neptune's clip of Phase 4 was rendered on 530168f and is therefore not byte equal to a render after Saturn's merge; the nine clips are made again from the master in Phase 6.

- Phase 5, the cause of frames that do not repeat (03:10 UTC on 2026-11-22). The Saturn agent found it on its own stop (`agent/saturn` 7dc2542, notes in `assets-src/saturn/NOTES.md` under "Item 8"): the harness GPU shades 2 x 2 pixel quads; a pixel that hit `discard` stops storing to variables, so a local first assigned after the discard holds stale memory, and `dFdx`, `dFdy`, `fwidth` and `texture()` without an explicit level read it for the live neighbours of the quad. Its haze shell began with a discard and later took `dFdx` inside the ring shadow. After its fix (no discard before the last statement, no cross pixel operation on a value first assigned in a per pixel branch) 3866, 3594, 3567 and 3840 gave one hash each in 11 renders over 3 fresh sessions, where 3866 gave 6 hashes in 12 renders before. What the Builder did with it: the engine agent's task 5 became an audit of every fragment shader for the pattern, shared code first, with a fix on `agent/engine-batch19` and a list per stop folder (MAIL 62); every stop agent got the rule for its own shaders with its next commit (MAIL 63, with the news that batch 18 is on main). G3 as the kit defines it (the first hold, dive, travel and terrain segment, fresh loads and reversed order) is green on main and does not sample the frames in question, so no machine check is red; the fix reaches main with Saturn's polish in Phase 6 and with batch 19 for shared code. - 05:27 UTC why the chain stopped at the preview film at 01:38 UTC, and the fix, which is in `tools/` only and changes no pixel. Finding: `npm run film -- --format preview --from-master` made a film of 5401 frames from a master of 5400 and refused it, rightly. The master's frame times were even (5400 packets, each 512 ticks after the last, 180.000 s), but its decode times were not: spans that x264 wrote with reordered frames (a delay of two frames) are joined without encoding to spans it wrote without any (spans of two frames), and at such a seam the mp4 holds a packet three frames long followed by packets one tick long; the join of 05:28 UTC counts the packets it had to give a new decode time or length: 229 in the film, all of them inside the clips (Mercury 22, Venus 67, Earth 46, Jupiter 57, Uranus 16, Neptune 21; none in the clips of the Sun, Mars and Saturn). A player shows every frame at its right time, so nothing was visible in the files as they were, but a converter that reads packet lengths at a constant rate repeats a frame at each seam and drops frames after it: measured on the old clips of Mercury, Jupiter and Neptune, a constant rate decode gave 496 frames for 495 with 346 frames out of place. That is what made the preview one frame long, and it is what a platform could do to a post when it encodes it again, at the very seam between the hold and the dive. Fix: `regularTiming` in `tools/lib/encode.ts`, called by every join without encoding (`concatCopy` for chunks, the film and the clips; `tools/post.ts` for a post). It reads the packet table, requires even frame times, and if a decode time or a packet length is uneven it writes the same stream once more with the same frame times and even decode times (one reorder delay for the whole file), then checks the result and throws if a frame time moved. No picture is encoded again. Proof on Mercury, Jupiter and Neptune: every decoded frame has the same hash before and after (495 of 495), the files differ by about 200 bytes of table, and a constant rate decode of the new file gives the same 495 frames in the same order. The first try (a pass through switch for the scaler) was refused by ffmpeg and dropped; a filter in the scaler alone was weighed and not chosen, because it would have left the clips and the posts as they were. The film and the nine clips are joined again from the same chunks, the film's every frame is compared by hash against the first join, and the eight posts made early are joined again by `npm run post`, as addendum 003 says for a clip that is remade. No intro is made again. The record of a joined file now carries `timing`.

- 2026-11-23 17:59 UTC, the blur in the dives and rises is capped by the shutter (E6, engine, mail 310). Measured: the first critics of rounds 37 and 40 score the judged dive and rise frames as smear (Earth 1857 "extreme radial zoom blur and low resolution stretching, blocky stepped streaks", severe; Earth 2156 "dragged into parallel streaks and do not hold detail at native size", severe; Mercury 1016 "smeared into long directional streaks", severe; Mercury 717 major), and the handover reports give the raw shutter motion at those frames as 29, 25, 77 and 59 px at the point that moves most, 25 to 80 px through most of every dive and rise. Cause: one steady move over a factor of about a hundred in 90 frames changes scale by 6 to 14 percent a frame, so the full shutter of `film.shutterDegrees` draws every small bright thing toward the frame edge as a flat ended dash; the path cannot be slower inside the timeline. Brandon's note names the blur first, so the place has to stay sharp on the way down. Decided: in a dive or rise of a stop that opted in, the shutter of a frame is shortened so the motion across it is at most `handover.maxBlurPx` at the point that moves most (start value 6), keeping the middle of the shutter, eased back to the full shutter over the last `handover.blurEaseFrames` of a rise so the travel after it meets no step. `film.shutterDegrees` and every frame outside those segments stay as they are; proof asked for at the review tier. Not a threshold of any check, no rubric and no judged frame changes. Known cost, not measured: with little blur the frame edges move 60 to 150 px from one frame to the next and may strobe in the video; the centre, where the place is, moves a few px. If Brandon sees strobing, the cap is one number in the config. The change goes onto main after rounds 38 and 39 are packed, before round 2 of any stop is judged.

- 2026-11-23 20:27 UTC, d140: the shutter inside a dive and a rise (E6) is set: `handover.maxBlurPx` 14 with `handover.minShutter` 0.5. In words: while the fastest point of the frame moves less than 14 px across the open shutter the shutter is whole (180 degrees, as everywhere else in the film); above that it closes so that the blur stays at 14 px, but never to less than half (90 degrees), so in the fastest frames the blur is half of what the whole shutter gives. Why not the whole shutter: on sharp ground it smears the picture where the dive is fastest (Earth 1882 at the review tier: the clouds at the lower right are streaks and the middle is soft; by the engineer's numbers Mars 2440 has 51 px at the middle of the right edge and 147 px at the corner), and that is the fault Brandon named first in his note ("it's a blurry mess"); the note outranks the kit where the two disagree. Why not a limit alone: the frames are sharp but lie far apart (at Mars 2430 three separate copies in a mean of three frames), which the motion critics of rounds 37 to 40 marked as major (Uranus 4126 to 4175) and which `kit/05-ARCHITECTURE.md` forbids ("Fast motion must come out as a smooth blur"). Why 0.5 and not 0.25: at 0.25 the streak is one eighth of the path between two frames (about 20 px of 160 at the rim of the Mars rise), the staccato of a 45 degree shutter; at 0.5 it is a quarter, the 90 degree shutter that film uses for fast action, with no separate copies (by the engineer's numbers 123 samples at Mars 2440 at the review and at the final tier, and 1.3 px in the middle of the frame). Seen by the Builder: Mars 2440 on main under five shutters (no difference to speak of, because the ground there is the soft globe map: the softness before the surface comes in is the map, and its cure is the place plates of each stop, not the shutter), Earth 1882 under four (the difference is plain), and the engineer's sheets of the Mars rise 2691 to 2693 at floor 0.25 and 0.5 on the eighth bake of the plates (the place stays sharp in the middle at both, and T cannot be named by the blur). This departs from `film.shutterDegrees` inside the dives and rises of stops that hand over and nowhere else: holds, terrain, travel and the ending keep the whole shutter, and the draft tier (one sample at the middle of the shutter) is untouched. Before it goes onto main the tree `builder/e6-on-main-42b1-c14-f50` 3004feba (main 42b1585c with the 21 engine files of `agent/engine-handover` aef36681 and the two numbers) must give the bytes of main on the 115 draft reference frames, on the 18 judged stills at the final tier, and on the 69 frames of the engineer's list at the review tier (the first and last frame of every hold, terrain, travel and ending segment, and frames of dives and rises that keep the whole shutter); those jobs are out (e6p, r69e, r69m). The number is one config key, so a round that shows the half shutter wrong on a stop can change it without an engine change.

(2) THE THIRD CURE is plan a: asin, acos and atan written out in basic operations as one definition inside the Neptune stop, called by every Neptune program on every renderer, so that the picture no longer rests on a platform's library. If it is more, plan b is taken: the written out functions are switched in only where the renderer is not the software renderer (through the material's onBeforeCompile hook, which hands over the renderer; a missing answer counts as a graphics card), so that the software text stays byte for byte and the approved picture bit for bit. Whole film, `mercury.travel`, judged frame 1072, R3 round 32 part 1, severe: "the second judged frame renders no solar surface, limb, or corona at all, showing only empty background starfield where the close-up or terrain view should be" The frame is the half way frame of the flight from Mercury to Venus and shows sky only: by the kit's travel rule the leaving body goes out behind the camera and the next body is a point of light until it grows. The critic had the Sun's frame 495 beside it and expected a body. The whole film critic names the same cause as a major (item 80), so it is kept as a severe and not argued away. Tried. Rounds 30 to 31 (engine batch 20): the flight sky as a star free band map with every star drawn as a point, each travel's band faded in across the turn. Rounds 31 to 32 (batches 21 and 22): the next body standing in its place as a point and growing on one eased curve over the last 33 frames (41 in the Sun's travel); with the band no longer filling the frame, 1072 became a plain star field. Next, Phase 6: a subject in the judged travel frames inside the kit's rule: the growth window opened earlier so that the next body is a small lit disc at the travel's half (trial on mercury.travel and uranus.travel, MAIL 145 job 3), and the plain field given a density that falls away from the galactic plane and clumps (`agent/flightsky` job 2, commit 4bb69be2); judged again by R3 on 1072 and by R5.
80. Whole film, the travels, frames 1072, 1642, 2212, 3352, 3922, 4492, R5 round 32, major: "Every planet runs the same four beats: a wide approach, a push in, a low pass over the surface, a pull out, then an empty starfield. With six nearly identical dead frames between stops, the film feels like a loop instead of one building journey." The same cause in round 31: "The views vary in subject, especially Saturn's ring skim, but the stops repeat the same large reveal, approach, close pass, pullback, and sky-only handoff already established in the inner planets. That predictability flattens the build." And in round 30: "Feature skims exist, but every stop feels the same: centered hero, near-duplicate push, one skim, then a Milky Way spacer. Jupiter barely advances between 2895 and 2997. Saturn's wide is repeated three times around the ring skim, and Titan jumps from the upper right to top center on the repeat. The sheet-05 holds are the same poster scale, dead center, stop after stop." Item 1 (blockout) is its first form. Tried: each stop its own approach side, dive path and terrain move (Phases 3 and 4); each travel its own turn side and angle; launches eased and arrivals pinned (batch 21); the steady growth of the next body (batch 22). Not changed: the five segments of a stop and their times, which are the kit's ("Every stop after the Sun has the same five segments") and Brandon's in the config, and the hold, which is the approved hero framing. Next, Phase 6: the travels made to differ in what they show at their half: the next body as a disc in some, the belt rock in mars.travel, the Sun in sun.travel and wherever a turn can pass it (MAIL 145 jobs 3 and 4); the stops' polish branches vary what moves inside the dive and the rise (Jupiter's dive trial). Judged again by R5.

At Mercury the Sun sits frame right and lights the right limb. Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn and Uranus are lit from the left. At Neptune (4605) the light is back on the right, from a sun in the upper right. The Sun's position does not follow one path through the film." Round 31: "The Sun goes from a huge clipped source at Mercury to no identifiable source across the middle holds, then returns as a bright point beside Neptune. The individual terminators mostly make sense, but the cut sequence does not let the viewer track the Sun shrinking or connect the lighting changes to one source." Round 30, severe: "The Sun does not shrink from stop to stop, and the light does not stay with it. It is a full disk, still a huge glaring disk at Mercury's upper right, then absent through Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and Uranus, then a pinpoint at Neptune's upper right. Key light flips from Mercury's right to the left for the middle holds, then back to the right at Neptune. Uranus and Neptune are exposed as bright as Earth, so distance never reads in the light. The same break starts earlier: sheet-01 frame 615 is keyed from the upper right, 1016 from the upper left with the Sun gone, and 1440 puts a large solar disk on the Venus horizon again." Tried. Nothing that moves a hold: the light's side at each hold is the approved hero image's ("Its direction is set per stop so the terminator falls where the approved hero image puts it", `kit/01-FILM.md`), and the exposure per stop is the kit's ("The outer planets are not dim"). 174. saturn, `saturn.hold 3465` and `saturn.terrain 3720`, R2, record round 36, fail (counts as one major), items 44 and 108 again: the judged hold and terrain frames drew 0 of 10 votes for "film or game cinematic" (hold b b e b b, terrain b b e b b) against 5 of 10 for the approved images in the stop's own control votes, collected once in round 13 (hold b a e a b, terrain a a e a b). The limit is a gap of 0.2, so 3 of 10 would pass. The same two frames from the same build of the stop (stop hash 47a787cd7f78408c in rounds 35 and 36) drew 3 of 10 from the jurors of round 35 and passed there; rounds 26 and 33 drew 2 and 1 of 10 and failed. The same two approved images drew 2 of 10 when the whole film rounds collected them once more in round 30, and against that the frames would pass; the kit reuses a stop's own collection, so the fail stands, as in item 108. Jurors on the hold: "The ring geometry is physically wrong: the rings don't pass in front of the planet's near side, and the planet looks like it's sitting on top of them.", "the polished, self-contained Saturn 'hero shot' composition, a generic illustration that reads more like stock space art than contextual cinematic imagery" and "Saturn's domain-warped FBM cloud swirls with embossed normal-mapped relief along the terminator (plus crisp 1D procedural ringlets with slight pixel aliasing) set against a noticeably softer equirectangular starfield skybox"; on the terrain view: "the real-time shader and alpha-blending artifact where the planet's glowing lit limb meets the semi-transparent inner rings, alongside high-frequency procedural noise and aliasing across the ring bands and cloud textures" and "generic unlabeled CGI beauty shot of Saturn with a flat textured ring disc". The whole film list passes R2 in this round: 19 of 135 votes against 18 of 90 for the controls. Tried: round 34 darkened the cream interior of the inner lanes through the hand over, hid the sky behind the unlit rings after the hold and widened the edge of the globe's shadow on the rings (item 121); round 35 put a tone field on the near lanes of the close picture (item 137). Neither was aimed at the jury, and the soft grooves and the meeting of the rings with the globe (items 39, 40 and 42) are as they were. Nothing follows: the record round scores the frozen build once and is not followed by fixes (kit/08, Phase 6 step 4), so this is open in the delivered build.

176. mars, `mars.rise 2690 to 2697`, `mars.rise 2722 to 2740`, `mars.dive 2434 to 2447` and `mars.rise 2690 to 2722`, measures on plan E's one move (em1, engine 6d260fb8, on main with d164), 2 severe. severe, `mars.rise 2690 to 2697` and `mars.rise 2722 to 2740`, smooth, speed of the picture: its change from one frame to the next is 0.097 of the move's mean at 2690.5 to 2697 and 0.089 at 2722 to 2740, against the limit of 0.08 (four red lines; the dive is green). Cause as the engineer explains it: the pitch term g = 1 - 0.333 cot(e) of the rise sets both places and no flank number cures it. Cure owed: a new law for the rise, by handover_engineer, as its own commit (mail 432). severe, G13 on 13 of 495 frames: 2434, 2440, 2446, 2447, 2690 to 2692, 2706, 2707, 2710, 2711, 2721 and 2722, worst 2707 at 4.37 percent soft against 2 percent. Cause: the plates of the place are too coarse for the lower path of the one move. Cure owed: the second bake of the country and the cap, by mars_place_builder. G5 and G17 pass and the handover report passes. Tried so far: nothing after this measure; both cures are in work. 02:06 UTC on 2026-11-24: the speed lines are cured at the cause by the rise's law, on main with d170 (largest step of the rise 0.074 against 0.08, the report of the path is green at whole frames and at rate 2). The G13 half stays open.

Entries 177 to 456 are every issue the record round left open: round 60, run 2 of 2, judged on main at 3fb8fc7 (engine hash a455bc02904b0d42), closed at 18:18 UTC on 2026-11-27. They are the 276 lines of "Issues, worst first" in `scorecards/round-060/SUMMARY.md`, in that order (severe first; 15 of them are the red lines of the smoothness measure), then the three stops that fail G13 and the one stop that fails R2. Each entry has the stop, the frame or frames, who found it, its words and the fix it names. The record round is not followed by fixes (kit/08, Phase 6), and Brandon's word of 2026-11-27 through Partner was to finish with no new quality rounds and no new look changes. So "Tried" says that nothing was tried after the round and names the earlier entries of this list whose first words name the same stop, where the work on that stop before the record round is written down.

- Round 1, Phase 2, blockout, whole film. R4 blockout 7, three major, two minor. Next: each stop arrives on its own curve, the approach starts earlier and eases longer, the lookback is reframed with a slow pan. `scorecards/round-001/`.
- Round 2, Phase 2, blockout, whole film. R4 blockout 5, one severe, four major, two minor. Limit reached. After the round: arrivals start off center, the lookback never stops moving, the turn away from Mars is longer. Open items 1 to 5. `scorecards/round-002/`.

- Round 4, Phase 3, mars, look lock round 2 of 5. Started 2026-11-20 UTC on main at 24c2334. Machine checks green before the pack (G1, G2 with 22 tests, G3, G4, G6, G7, G10, G11, G12, G14, G15). The join at the rise cover was severe in round 6 as well, so by the plateau rule the technique changes: ladder "A cover can be seen as a join", rung 1 done on the geometry (one Sun direction for the whole stop, the limb line, the Sun and the ring arcs at the same place on both sides of the swap frame) and rung 2 (a thicker cover that moves with the camera); after the swap one eased pull back on one curve with the Sun, the rings and the stars fixed in the world, and a sky that stays alive to the last frame. (2) Dive, 4142 to 4150: the picture jumps before the cover (the Sun pops in, the ring streaks change sides, the limb flattens and darkens, the Milky Way drops out within eight frames); the swap belongs under the full cover and the approach bends toward the terrain pose before it. (3) Dive, 4118 to 4134: the speed steps up after a near still hold; eased in over thirty frames or more. (4) Stepped copies: at the rise cover's exit the Sun stands as two blobs and the ring arcs as double lines (4413 to 4416, two pictures of the same things at two places), and under the dive cover the bright limb shows through in stacked copies (4159 to 4161); the engine's sample count under a translucent cover is in work on the engine side. (5) Dive cover exit, 4167 to 4170: the Sun goes from absent to full flare and the rings from invisible to crisp within three frames; the clearing is stretched to ten frames or more. (6) Match at 4290: the right ring arc as thick flat white strokes without the approved strands and tint, dark dots along the inner ringlet, the fine inner ringlets fading out before the limb; a thin hard line along the disc's edge inside the cyan glow. Match at 4035: the right moon a quarter too large, both moons with cut out rims, even noise for craters and black night sides without planetshine. (7) Craft, plateau (named in rounds 6 and 21): the cloud deck is smeared into parallel streaks with nothing fine in it (4137, 4290, 4436); ladder "A globe looks plastic, flat or like a web demo", rung 3 (cloud flecks as their own layer with soft shadows) with rung 1 (fine relief). The moon at 4436 is a soft oval. (8) Brandon's order on the terrain view: 4200 to 4379 moves as one plane with weak depth (minor for the critic, first rank here); more forward travel, lower, with a nearer cloud layer. Minors: the hold's turn and drift barely visible; ring strands and Milky Way core softer than approved; the flare streak short; a ring tip like a needle at the horizon; the white rim as an outline over the halo at 4436; stars as dashes right of the rings at 4290. R1 stays 7, R3 rose from 5 to 6, R4 stays 4, R2 passes (0 of 10 against 1 of 10 for the controls), R8 passes. Summary in `scorecards/round-021/`.

- Round 24, Phase 4, sun, round 3 of 3. Started 2026-11-21 18:20 UTC. Judged on main at 530168f. Measures green. R1 9, R2 pass, R3 5, R4 6, R8 pass. 0 severe, 11 major. All four severe issues of round 15 are gone: the kaleidoscope seams behind the sunspot are down to one major, the vertical tile seam in the Milky Way at 247 and the cut through a whiteout at the rise cover are not reported, and the black moat round the glow is down to a minor. In the pullback the far side is smeared, the cap is blown out and there is no soft terminator (2726). The shadowed canyon ground is muddy and the horizon glow is a flat hot band, both as in the approved image (2580). Minors: the moon leaves the dive too fast, its edge is stepped and it is softer than the planet, the foreground rock is slightly soft. Carried: the pullback shows Mars lit from below with north to the left, the turn toward Jupiter banks about 90 degrees, and the moon is not in the pullback.
    ```
    What I would improve next: The two handovers first: carry the speed of the plunge into the first second of the canyon view, and let the dust of the climb stream with the camera and thin over ten frames or more so the limb grows into view.
    Then the limb: one haze layer drawn across the edge of the disc, and a faint blue rim on the night side.
    Then the pullback: repaint the far side of the map at the detail of the dive patches, rebuild the cap on a polar projection and lower its exposure.
    To continue: send the resume prompt from kit/10-KICKOFF.md
    ```

The limit is 34 dB and 0.93. No render has started. 2. The cause of the rest is found, and MEASURED by me on your PC's own full size frame (picture 3). Direct3D, the graphics layer of Windows, writes two angle functions (asin and atan) as short formulas that are wrong by up to 0.00007 rad, with a small step at zero. Neptune's clouds are laid out with these angles times the planet's radius, so on the PC the fine cloud pattern sits 1 to 2 pixels off in about a third of the frame (MEASURED: 42 of 144 blocks of the surface view, 36 of 144 of the flight out). The eye hardly sees that in the side by side; the test's second measure does. Put into the cloud's drawing by hand, the same formulas give your PC's picture: your PC's frame agrees with that drawing at 39.41 dB and 0.9650, and with the unchanged drawing only at 34.23 dB and 0.9282. So what I called fine grain that falls differently at 12:00 AM was a wrong reading: it has a cause and it can be cured. No limit of their own for Neptune's frames is planned. 3. The third cure is in work since 12:06 AM: the angle functions written out in plain arithmetic inside the Neptune stop, the same on every machine. One thing to know before it lands: with it the cloud's own drawing can no longer be proven bit for bit the same as before, because written out functions and built in ones round differently in the last digit. I expect one brightness level in a few pixels; I measure it on whole frames and name the numbers with the commit. If it is more than that, I take the second way: only graphics cards get the written out functions and the cloud keeps its own, so the approved picture stays bit for bit. 4.
